elements.id-string-7: Discontinuities and delayed terms are encountered in the governing equations of a large class of problems ranging from physics, engineering, medicine to economics.
elements.id-string-8: These systems are impossible to be properly modelled and simulated with standard Ordinary Differential Equations (ODE), or any data-driven approximation including Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODE).
elements.id-string-9: To circumvent this issue, latent variables are typically introduced to solve the dynamics of the system in a higher dimensional space and obtain the solution as a projection to the original space.
elements.id-string-10: However, this solution lacks physical interpretability.
elements.id-string-11: In contrast, Delay Differential Equations (DDEs) and their data-driven, approximated counterparts naturally appear as good candidates to characterize such complicated systems.
elements.id-string-12: In this work we revisit the recently proposed Neural DDE by introducing Neural State-Dependent DDE (SDDDE), a general and flexible framework featuring multiple and state-dependent delays.
elements.id-string-13: The developed framework is auto-differentiable and runs efficiently on multiple backends.
elements.id-string-14: We show that our method is competitive and outperforms other continuous-class models on a wide variety of delayed dynamical systems.

elements.id-string-131: In the following, we discuss similarities, drawbacks and benefits of Neural SDDDE compared with the following models: NODE, ANODE and Neural Laplace.
elements.id-string-132: Compared to these techniques, we recall that Neural SDDDE is a direct method for solving DDEs, specifically designed to handle delayed systems; it does not require lifting of the problem to higher-dimensional spaces, with the benefit of preserving physical interpretability.
elements.id-string-133: This is not the case for ANODE, the augmented version of ODE, where flexibility is obtained by introducing an higher dimentional space.
elements.id-string-134: Lastly, Neural Laplace can solve a broader class of differential equations, although with some limitations that we pinpoint in the following.
elements.id-string-136: Neural Laplace is a model that needs memory initialized latent variables, i.e., a long portion of the trajectory needs to be fed in order to get a reasonable representation of the latent variable.
elements.id-string-137: In contrast, by design, NODE and ANODE require information only at the initial time to predict the system dynamics.
elements.id-string-138: From this viewpoint, Neural SDDDE is somewhat a hybrid approach since a history function $\phi(t)$ is required.
elements.id-string-139: $\phi$ needs to be provided for $t\in[-\tau_{\mathrm{max}},0]$, where $\tau_{\mathrm{max}}$ is the maximum delay encountered during integration.
elements.id-string-140: This is more restricting than solely relying on an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(0)$ but far less than memory-based latent variables methods.
elements.id-string-141: Moreover, the training and testing schemes for Neural Laplace is constrained by this very same observation since future events can only be predicted after a certain observation time.
elements.id-string-142: This also makes the length of the trajectory to feed to Neural Laplace a hyperparameter to tune.
elements.id-string-143: This is not the case with NODE, ANODE and our approach.
elements.id-string-145: \paragraph{Memory complexity} DDE integration necessitates keeping a record of all previous states in memory due to the presence of delayed terms.
elements.id-string-146: This is because at any given time $t$, the DDE solver must be able to accurately determine $\mathbf{x}(t-\tau)$ through interpolation of the stored state history.
elements.id-string-147: This extra amount of extra memory needed depends on the solver used.
elements.id-string-148: For example, the additional memory required when using a RK solver for one trajectory is $O(SNd)$.
elements.id-string-149: The model's memory footprint is not affected by the number of delays.
elements.id-string-150: \paragraph{Time complexity} In comparison to NODE, the solution estimate $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}$ needs to be evaluated for each delayed state argument, i.e., $\mathbf{x}(t-\tau_i)$.
elements.id-string-151: The cost of evaluating the interpolant is small compared to the cost of computing its coefficients.
elements.id-string-152: Similarly, the time complexity is conditioned by the solver used.
elements.id-string-153: For example, for a RK scheme, the coefficient computation scales linearly with the number of stages.
elements.id-string-154: Hence, Neural SDDDE adds a time cost $O(SD\,d)$ compared to NODE for each vector field function evaluation.

elements.id-string-446: In this paper, we introduced Neural State-Dependent Delays Differential Equations (Neural SDDDE) capable of solving DDEs with any type of delays via neural networks.
elements.id-string-447: This open-source, robust python DDE solver compatible with neural networks pushes the current envelope of Neural DDEs by handling the delays in a more generic way.
elements.id-string-448: To the best of our knowledge, no machine learning library or open-sourced code is available to model such a large class of DDEs.
elements.id-string-449: To validate the effectiveness of Neural SDDDE, we conducted a series of benchmark tests, comparing it against NODEs, the augmented version ANODE, and Neural Laplace.
elements.id-string-450: These numerical experiments covered a diverse range of models, including time- and state-dependent scenarios, as well as a delayed Partial Differential Equation (PDE).
elements.id-string-451: Our findings revealed that Neural SDDDE accurately reproduced the dynamics across all scenarios tested.
elements.id-string-452: Furthermore, Neural SDDDE demonstrated superior performance in terms of accuracy and reliability when compared to the other established methods.
elements.id-string-453: We believe this flexible and versatile tool may provide a valuable contribution to several fields such as control theory where time-delay are often considered.
